questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solid sphere of mass 5 kg and a disc of mass 4 kg have the same radius. The ratio of moment of inertia of the sphere about its tangent to the moment of inertia of the disc about a tangent in its plane will be $x : y$. The value of $x$ and $y$ respectively is
questions.solution:
Mass of the solid sphere, $M_s = 5$ kg
Mass of the disc, $M_d = 4$ kg
Let the radius of both the sphere and the disc be $R$.

The moment of inertia of a solid sphere about its tangent is obtained using the parallel axis theorem:
$I_s = I_{cm} + M_s R^2 = \dfrac{2}{5} M_s R^2 + M_s R^2 = \dfrac{7}{5} M_s R^2$
Substituting $M_s = 5$ kg:
$I_s = \dfrac{7}{5} \times 5 \times R^2 = 7 R^2$

The moment of inertia of a disc about a tangent in its plane is also obtained using the parallel axis theorem (shifting from the diameter):
$I_d = I_{diameter} + M_d R^2 = \dfrac{1}{4} M_d R^2 + M_d R^2 = \dfrac{5}{4} M_d R^2$
Substituting $M_d = 4$ kg:
$I_d = \dfrac{5}{4} \times 4 \times R^2 = 5 R^2$

The ratio of their moments of inertia is:
$\dfrac{I_s}{I_d} = \dfrac{7 R^2}{5 R^2} = \dfrac{7}{5}$

Comparing this with $x : y$, we get $x = 7$ and $y = 5$.

Answer: $7, 5$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body is rotating about its own axis. Its rotational kinetic energy is '$x$' and its angular momentum is '$y$'. Hence its moment of inertia about its own axis is
questions.solution:
Rotational kinetic energy is given by $K = \dfrac{L^2}{2I}$

Substituting the given values, $K = x$ and $L = y$

$x = \dfrac{y^2}{2I}$

$I = \dfrac{y^2}{2x}$

Answer: $\dfrac{y^2}{2x}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two identical rings A and B of same mass and radius are revolving, ring A arounds its own diameter and ring B about tangential axis in its own plane. Both the rings A and B have same rotational kinetic energy. The ratio of the angular velocity of ring B to that of ring A is
questions.solution:
Moment of inertia of ring A about its diameter is $I_A = \dfrac{1}{2}MR^2$.

Moment of inertia of ring B about a tangential axis in its own plane is obtained using the parallel axis theorem:
$I_B = I_A + MR^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}MR^2 + MR^2 = \dfrac{3}{2}MR^2$.

Rotational kinetic energy is given by $K = \dfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2$.

Given that both rings have the same rotational kinetic energy, $K_A = K_B$:
$\dfrac{1}{2}I_A\omega_A^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}I_B\omega_B^2$

$\dfrac{\omega_B^2}{\omega_A^2} = \dfrac{I_A}{I_B}$

$\dfrac{\omega_B}{\omega_A} = \sqrt{\dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2}MR^2}{\dfrac{3}{2}MR^2}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{3}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$

The ratio of the angular velocity of ring B to that of ring A is $1 : \sqrt{3}$.

Answer: $1 : \sqrt{3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solid sphere rolls down from the top of an inclined plane. On reaching the bottom of the plane, its velocity is '$V_1$'. When the same sphere slides down from the top of the same plane of same height, its velocity on reaching the bottom is '$V_2$'. The ratio $V_1 : V_2$ is (neglect friction)
questions.solution:
When a solid sphere rolls down an inclined plane of height $h$, by conservation of mechanical energy:

$mgh = \dfrac{1}{2}mV_1^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2$

For a solid sphere, the moment of inertia is $I = \dfrac{2}{5}mr^2$ and for pure rolling, $\omega = \dfrac{V_1}{r}$.

$mgh = \dfrac{1}{2}mV_1^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{2}{5}mr^2\right)\left(\dfrac{V_1}{r}\right)^2$

$mgh = \dfrac{1}{2}mV_1^2 + \dfrac{1}{5}mV_1^2 = \dfrac{7}{10}mV_1^2$

$V_1 = \sqrt{\dfrac{10gh}{7}}$

When the sphere slides down the same plane without friction, it only acquires translational kinetic energy. By conservation of mechanical energy:

$mgh = \dfrac{1}{2}mV_2^2$

$V_2 = \sqrt{2gh}$

The ratio of the velocities is:

$\dfrac{V_1}{V_2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{\dfrac{10gh}{7}}}{\sqrt{2gh}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{10}{7 \times 2}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{5}{7}}$

Thus, $V_1 : V_2 = \sqrt{5} : \sqrt{7}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A force of $3\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k}$ N acts on a particle with position vector $\hat{i} + \hat{j} - \hat{k}$ m. The magnitude of torque of given force is
questions.solution:
Given force $\vec{F} = 3\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k}$ N

Position vector $\vec{r} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} - \hat{k}$ m

Torque $\vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F}$

$\vec{\tau} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \ 1 & 1 & -1 \ 3 & 2 & -1 \end{vmatrix}$

$\vec{\tau} = \hat{i}(-1 - (-2)) - \hat{j}(-1 - (-3)) + \hat{k}(2 - 3)$

$\vec{\tau} = \hat{i} - 2\hat{j} - \hat{k}$

Magnitude of torque $|\vec{\tau}| = \sqrt{1^2 + (-2)^2 + (-1)^2} = \sqrt{1 + 4 + 1} = \sqrt{6}$ N m

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The radius of gyration of a solid sphere of radius 'R' and mass 'M' about its diameter is $K_d$ and that about a tangent of a solid sphere is $K_t$. The ratio of $K_d$ to $K_t$ is
questions.solution:
The moment of inertia of a solid sphere about its diameter is $I_d = \dfrac{2}{5}MR^2$.

The radius of gyration about the diameter is $K_d = \sqrt{\dfrac{2}{5}}R$.

Using the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia of the solid sphere about a tangent is $I_t = I_d + MR^2 = \dfrac{2}{5}MR^2 + MR^2 = \dfrac{7}{5}MR^2$.

The radius of gyration about the tangent is $K_t = \sqrt{\dfrac{7}{5}}R$.

The ratio of $K_d$ to $K_t$ is $\dfrac{K_d}{K_t} = \dfrac{\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{5}}R}{\sqrt{\dfrac{7}{5}}R} = \left(\dfrac{2}{7}\right)^{1/2}$.

Answer: $\left(\dfrac{2}{7}\right)^{1/2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A thin uniform rod AB of mass '$m$' and length '$l$' is hinged at one end A to the ground level. Initially the rod stands vertically and is allowed to fall freely to the ground in the vertical plane. The angular velocity of the rod when its B end strikes the ground is
($g$ = acceleration due to gravity)
questions.solution:
By the principle of conservation of mechanical energy, the loss in potential energy of the rod is equal to the gain in its rotational kinetic energy.

The initial height of the center of mass of the rod is $h_i = \dfrac{l}{2}$ and the final height is $h_f = 0$.

Loss in potential energy $= mg\left(\dfrac{l}{2}\right)$

Gain in rotational kinetic energy $= \dfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2$

The moment of inertia of the rod about the hinged end A is $I = \dfrac{ml^2}{3}$.

Equating the two energies:

$mg\left(\dfrac{l}{2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{ml^2}{3}\right)\omega^2$

$mgl = \dfrac{ml^2}{3}\omega^2$

$\omega^2 = \dfrac{3g}{l}$

$\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{3g}{l}}$

Answer: $\sqrt{\dfrac{3g}{l}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solid sphere rolls without slipping on an inclied plane at an angle $\theta$. The ratio of total kinetic energy to its rotational kinetic energy is
questions.solution:
For a solid sphere rolling without slipping, the velocity of the center of mass $v$ and angular velocity $\omega$ are related by $v = \omega R$.

The translational kinetic energy is $K_{trans} = \dfrac{1}{2} m v^2$.

The rotational kinetic energy is $K_{rot} = \dfrac{1}{2} I \omega^2$.

Substituting the moment of inertia of a solid sphere $I = \dfrac{2}{5} m R^2$ and $\omega = \dfrac{v}{R}$:

$K_{rot} = \dfrac{1}{2} \left(\dfrac{2}{5} m R^2\right) \left(\dfrac{v}{R}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{5} m v^2$

The total kinetic energy is the sum of translational and rotational kinetic energies:

$K_{total} = K_{trans} + K_{rot} = \dfrac{1}{2} m v^2 + \dfrac{1}{5} m v^2 = \dfrac{7}{10} m v^2$

The ratio of total kinetic energy to rotational kinetic energy is:

$\dfrac{K_{total}}{K_{rot}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{7}{10} m v^2}{\dfrac{1}{5} m v^2} = \dfrac{7}{2}$

Answer: $\dfrac{7}{2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A kathak dancer is standing on horizontal surface with folded hands. In the begining dancer is rotating about his central axis and his kinetic energy is 'K' at that time. The kathak dancer now stretches his arms so that the moment of inertia of the dancer becomes three times and the angular velocity becomes one-third. The kinetic energy of the dancer now is
questions.solution:
Initial kinetic energy of the dancer is given by $K = \dfrac{1}{2} I \omega^2$

When the dancer stretches his arms, the new moment of inertia becomes $I' = 3I$ and the new angular velocity becomes $\omega' = \dfrac{\omega}{3}$

The new kinetic energy is $K' = \dfrac{1}{2} I' \omega'^2$

Substituting the values of $I'$ and $\omega'$:

$K' = \dfrac{1}{2} (3I) \left(\dfrac{\omega}{3}\right)^2$

$K' = \dfrac{1}{2} (3I) \left(\dfrac{\omega^2}{9}\right)$

$K' = \dfrac{1}{3} \left(\dfrac{1}{2} I \omega^2\right)$

$K' = \dfrac{K}{3}$

Answer: $\dfrac{K}{3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Given identical rings are arranged in a hexagonal plane pattern so as to touch each neighbouring ring as shown in figure. Each ring has mass M and radius R. The moment of inertia of the system of seven rings about an axis passing through the centre of central ring and normal to plane of all rings is
questions.solution:
The moment of inertia of the central ring about the axis passing through its centre and perpendicular to its plane is:

$I_0 = MR^2$

For each of the six surrounding rings, the distance from its centre to the central axis is $d = 2R$.

Using the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia of one surrounding ring about the central axis is:

$I_1 = I_{cm} + Md^2$

$I_1 = MR^2 + M(2R)^2$

$I_1 = MR^2 + 4MR^2 = 5MR^2$

Since there are six identical surrounding rings, their total moment of inertia about the central axis is:

$I_{surrounding} = 6 \times I_1 = 6 \times 5MR^2 = 30MR^2$

The total moment of inertia of the system of seven rings is the sum of the moment of inertia of the central ring and the surrounding rings:

$I_{total} = I_0 + I_{surrounding}$

$I_{total} = MR^2 + 30MR^2 = 31MR^2$

Answer: $31MR^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The radius of gyration K of a hollow sphere of mass M and radius R about an axis XY is equal to R as shown in figure. The distance of that axis from the center of the sphere is h. The value of h is
questions.solution:
The moment of inertia of a hollow sphere about an axis passing through its center is given by:

$I_{CM} = \dfrac{2}{3}MR^2$

Using the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia about the axis $XY$ at a distance $h$ from the center is:

$I_{XY} = I_{CM} + Mh^2$

$I_{XY} = \dfrac{2}{3}MR^2 + Mh^2$

The radius of gyration $K$ about the axis $XY$ is given as $R$. Therefore, the moment of inertia can also be written as:

$I_{XY} = MK^2 = MR^2$

Equating the two expressions for $I_{XY}$:

$MR^2 = \dfrac{2}{3}MR^2 + Mh^2$

$h^2 = R^2 - \dfrac{2}{3}R^2$

$h^2 = \dfrac{1}{3}R^2$

$h = \dfrac{R}{\sqrt{3}}$

Answer: $\dfrac{R}{\sqrt{3}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solid cylinder and a solid sphere having the same mass and radius roll down on the same smooth inclined plane. The ratio of the acceleration of the cylinder $(a_c)$ to that of the sphere $(a_s)$ is
questions.solution:
The acceleration of a body rolling down an inclined plane is given by $a = \dfrac{g \sin \theta}{1 + \dfrac{I}{MR^2}}$.

For a solid cylinder, $I_c = \dfrac{1}{2}MR^2$.

$a_c = \dfrac{g \sin \theta}{1 + \dfrac{1}{2}} = \dfrac{2}{3}g \sin \theta$

For a solid sphere, $I_s = \dfrac{2}{5}MR^2$.

$a_s = \dfrac{g \sin \theta}{1 + \dfrac{2}{5}} = \dfrac{5}{7}g \sin \theta$

The ratio of the acceleration of the cylinder to that of the sphere is:

$\dfrac{a_c}{a_s} = \dfrac{\dfrac{2}{3}g \sin \theta}{\dfrac{5}{7}g \sin \theta} = \dfrac{14}{15}$

Answer: $\dfrac{14}{15}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The angular momentum of a rotating body is 'L'. When the frequency of rotating body is tripled and its kinetic energy is made one-third, the new angular momentum becomes
questions.solution:
The kinetic energy of a rotating body is given by $K = \dfrac{1}{2} L \omega$

Since $\omega = 2 \pi f$, we can write $K = \pi L f$

Therefore, the angular momentum is $L = \dfrac{K}{\pi f}$

Given that the new frequency is $f' = 3f$ and the new kinetic energy is $K' = \dfrac{K}{3}$

The new angular momentum is $L' = \dfrac{K'}{\pi f'} = \dfrac{\dfrac{K}{3}}{\pi (3f)} = \dfrac{1}{9} \dfrac{K}{\pi f} = \dfrac{L}{9}$

Answer: $\dfrac{L}{9}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A mass tied to a string is whirled in a horizontal circular path with a constant angular velocity and its angular momentum is 'L'. If the length of the string is now halved, keeping angular velocity same then the angular momentum will be
questions.solution:
The angular momentum of a particle of mass $m$ moving in a circle of radius $r$ with angular velocity $\omega$ is given by $L = I\omega = mr^2\omega$.

Given that the initial angular momentum is $L = mr^2\omega$.

When the length of the string is halved, the new radius becomes $r' = \dfrac{r}{2}$.

The angular velocity $\omega$ is kept constant.

The new angular momentum is $L' = m(r')^2\omega = m\left(\dfrac{r}{2}\right)^2\omega = \dfrac{mr^2\omega}{4}$.

Substituting the initial angular momentum, we get $L' = \dfrac{L}{4}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{L}{4}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solid sphere of radius R and mass M is rotating about its diameter. The moment of intertia of the solid sphere rotating about an axis at a distance $\dfrac{R}{3}$ from the centre and parallel to that diameter is
questions.solution:
The moment of inertia of a solid sphere of mass $M$ and radius $R$ about its diameter (an axis passing through its centre) is given by:

$I_{cm} = \dfrac{2}{5}MR^2$

Using the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia $I$ about an axis parallel to the diameter and at a distance $d = \dfrac{R}{3}$ from the centre is:

$I = I_{cm} + Md^2$

Substituting the values:

$I = \dfrac{2}{5}MR^2 + M\left(\dfrac{R}{3}\right)^2$

$I = \dfrac{2}{5}MR^2 + \dfrac{1}{9}MR^2$

$I = \left(\dfrac{18 + 5}{45}\right)MR^2$

$I = \dfrac{23}{45}MR^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Radius of gyration of a thin uniform circular disc about the axis passing through its centre and perpendicular to its plane is $K_c$. Radius of gyration of the same disc about a diamter of the disc is $K_d$. the ratio $K_d : K_c$ is
questions.solution:
Moment of inertia of a uniform circular disc about an axis passing through its centre and perpendicular to its plane is $I_c = \dfrac{1}{2}MR^2$.

Radius of gyration $K_c = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_c}{M}} = \dfrac{R}{\sqrt{2}}$.

Moment of inertia of the disc about its diameter is $I_d = \dfrac{1}{4}MR^2$.

Radius of gyration $K_d = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_d}{M}} = \dfrac{R}{2}$.

Ratio $\dfrac{K_d}{K_c} = \dfrac{\dfrac{R}{2}}{\dfrac{R}{\sqrt{2}}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$.

Thus, $K_d : K_c = 1 : \sqrt{2}$.

Answer: $1 : \sqrt{2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two bodies A and B have moment of inertia $I_A$ and $I_B$, and angular momenta $L_A$ and $L_B$ respectively. Both of them have same kinetic energy of rotation. So the ratio $L_A$ to $L_B$ is
questions.solution:
The rotational kinetic energy of a body is given by $K = \dfrac{L^2}{2I}$, where $L$ is the angular momentum and $I$ is the moment of inertia.

Given that both bodies have the same rotational kinetic energy, $K_A = K_B$.

$\dfrac{L_A^2}{2I_A} = \dfrac{L_B^2}{2I_B}$

$\dfrac{L_A^2}{L_B^2} = \dfrac{I_A}{I_B}$

Taking the square root on both sides, we get:

$\dfrac{L_A}{L_B} = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_A}{I_B}}$

Answer: $\sqrt{\dfrac{I_A}{I_B}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A system of five solid spheres each of mass '$m$' and radius '$r$' are rotating about an axis AA' as shown in figure. Hence the moment of inertia of the system about the axis of rotation AA' is
questions.solution:
The system consists of $5$ solid spheres, each of mass $m$ and radius $r$.

From the given figure, the axis of rotation AA' passes through the centers of $3$ spheres (one at the top and two at the bottom).

The moment of inertia of a solid sphere about an axis passing through its center is $I_{cm} = \dfrac{2}{5}mr^2$.

Total moment of inertia for these $3$ spheres is:

$I_1 = 3 \times \dfrac{2}{5}mr^2 = \dfrac{6}{5}mr^2$

The remaining $2$ spheres are placed such that they touch each other, and the axis AA' passes through their point of contact. Thus, the distance of their centers from the axis AA' is $r$.

Using the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia of one such sphere about the axis AA' is:

$I_{off} = I_{cm} + mr^2 = \dfrac{2}{5}mr^2 + mr^2 = \dfrac{7}{5}mr^2$

Total moment of inertia for these $2$ spheres is:

$I_2 = 2 \times \dfrac{7}{5}mr^2 = \dfrac{14}{5}mr^2$

The total moment of inertia of the system about the axis AA' is the sum of the moments of inertia of all $5$ spheres:

$I = I_1 + I_2 = \dfrac{6}{5}mr^2 + \dfrac{14}{5}mr^2 = \dfrac{20}{5}mr^2 = 4mr^2$

Answer: $4\ mr^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Four point masses m, 2m, 3m and 4m are kept at the corners A, B, C and D respectively of a square ABCD of side '$b$'. The moment of inertia of the system about an axis perpendicular to the plane of the square and passing through the point D is
questions.solution:
The moment of inertia of a system of point masses is given by $I = \sum m_i r_i^2$, where $r_i$ is the perpendicular distance of the $i$-th mass from the axis of rotation.

The axis of rotation is perpendicular to the plane of the square and passes through point D. The distances of the masses from the axis are:

For mass at A ($m_A = m$): $r_A = b$

For mass at B ($m_B = 2m$): $r_B = b\sqrt{2}$ (diagonal of the square)

For mass at C ($m_C = 3m$): $r_C = b$

For mass at D ($m_D = 4m$): $r_D = 0$

Substituting these values into the formula:

$I = m(b)^2 + 2m(b\sqrt{2})^2 + 3m(b)^2 + 4m(0)^2$

$I = mb^2 + 2m(2b^2) + 3mb^2 + 0$

$I = mb^2 + 4mb^2 + 3mb^2 = 8mb^2$

Answer: $8\ mb^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Solid sphere is rotating about an axis as shown in figure. If the radius of the sphere is 5 cm, then radius of gyration about that axis will be $\sqrt{x}$ cm. The value of x is
questions.solution:
The moment of inertia of a solid sphere about an axis passing through its center of mass is given by $I_{cm} = \dfrac{2}{5}MR^2$.

Using the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia about the given axis of rotation is:

$I = I_{cm} + Md^2$

where $d$ is the distance from the axis of rotation to the center of mass of the sphere.

Given $R = 5$ cm and $d = 10$ cm, we have:

$I = \dfrac{2}{5}M(5)^2 + M(10)^2$

$I = 10M + 100M = 110M$

The radius of gyration $k$ is defined by $I = Mk^2$.

$Mk^2 = 110M$

$k^2 = 110$

$k = \sqrt{110}$ cm

Comparing this with $\sqrt{x}$ cm, we get $x = 110$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform solid cylinder with radius R and length L has moment of inertia $I_1$ about the axis of the cylinder. A concentric solid cylinder of radius $R/2$ and length $L/2$ is carved out of the original cylinder. If $I_2$ is the moment of inertia of the carved out portion of the cylinder then $I_1/I_2$ is (Both $I_1$ and $I_2$ are about the axis of the cylinder)
questions.solution:
Let the density of the material of the cylinder be $\rho$.

The mass of the original solid cylinder is $M_1 = \rho \pi R^2 L$.
The moment of inertia of the original solid cylinder about its axis is:
$I_1 = \dfrac{1}{2} M_1 R^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} (\rho \pi R^2 L) R^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \rho \pi R^4 L$

The carved out portion is a solid cylinder of radius $R/2$ and length $L/2$. Its mass is:
$M_2 = \rho \pi \left(\dfrac{R}{2}\right)^2 \left(\dfrac{L}{2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{8} \rho \pi R^2 L$

The moment of inertia of this carved out portion about the same axis is:
$I_2 = \dfrac{1}{2} M_2 \left(\dfrac{R}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \left(\dfrac{1}{8} \rho \pi R^2 L\right) \left(\dfrac{R^2}{4}\right) = \dfrac{1}{64} \rho \pi R^4 L$

Taking the ratio of $I_1$ to $I_2$:
$\dfrac{I_1}{I_2} = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2} \rho \pi R^4 L}{\dfrac{1}{64} \rho \pi R^4 L} = 32$

Thus, the ratio is $32 : 1$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solid sphere of mass M and a disc of mass $\dfrac{M}{2}$ have the same radius. The ratio of moment of inertia of the disc about a tangent in its plane to the moment of inertia of the sphere about its tangent will be
questions.solution:
Let the radius of the solid sphere and the disc be $R$.

Mass of the solid sphere, $m_{s} = M$

Mass of the disc, $m_{d} = \dfrac{M}{2}$

Moment of inertia of the disc about its diameter is $\dfrac{1}{4}m_{d}R^2$. Using the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia of the disc about a tangent in its plane is:

$I_{disc} = \dfrac{1}{4}m_{d}R^2 + m_{d}R^2 = \dfrac{5}{4}m_{d}R^2$

Substituting $m_{d} = \dfrac{M}{2}$:

$I_{disc} = \dfrac{5}{4}\left(\dfrac{M}{2}\right)R^2 = \dfrac{5}{8}MR^2$

Moment of inertia of the solid sphere about its diameter is $\dfrac{2}{5}m_{s}R^2$. Using the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia of the solid sphere about its tangent is:

$I_{sphere} = \dfrac{2}{5}m_{s}R^2 + m_{s}R^2 = \dfrac{7}{5}m_{s}R^2$

Substituting $m_{s} = M$:

$I_{sphere} = \dfrac{7}{5}MR^2$

The required ratio is:

$\dfrac{I_{disc}}{I_{sphere}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{5}{8}MR^2}{\dfrac{7}{5}MR^2} = \dfrac{5}{8} \times \dfrac{5}{7} = \dfrac{25}{56}$

Answer: $25 : 56$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A Solid sphere has mass M and radius R. Its moment of inertia about a parallel axis passing through a point at a distance R/3 from its centre is
questions.solution:
The moment of inertia of a solid sphere about an axis passing through its centre is $I_{cm} = \dfrac{2}{5}MR^2$.

Using the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia about a parallel axis at a distance $d$ from the centre is given by $I = I_{cm} + Md^2$.

Given $d = \dfrac{R}{3}$, substituting the values:

$I = \dfrac{2}{5}MR^2 + M\left(\dfrac{R}{3}\right)^2$

$I = \dfrac{2}{5}MR^2 + \dfrac{1}{9}MR^2$

$I = \left(\dfrac{18 + 5}{45}\right)MR^2$

$I = \dfrac{23}{45}MR^2$

Answer: $23\text{MR}^2/45$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If the earth suddenly contracts to $\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{rd}$ of its present size without change in its mass, the ratio kinetic energy of the earth after and before contraction will be (Earth is assumed to be a rotating sphere about itself)
questions.solution:
By conservation of angular momentum, $L_1 = L_2$.

The rotational kinetic energy is given by $K = \dfrac{L^2}{2I}$.

The ratio of final to initial kinetic energy is $\dfrac{K_2}{K_1} = \dfrac{I_1}{I_2}$.

The moment of inertia of a solid sphere is $I = \dfrac{2}{5}MR^2$.

Given $R_2 = \dfrac{R_1}{3}$, we have $I_2 = \dfrac{2}{5}M\left(\dfrac{R_1}{3}\right)^2 = \dfrac{I_1}{9}$.

Therefore, $\dfrac{K_2}{K_1} = \dfrac{I_1}{\dfrac{I_1}{9}} = 9$.

Answer: $9$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The power (P) is supplied to rotating body having moment of inertia 'I' and angular acceleration '$\alpha$'. Its instantaneous angular velocity is
questions.solution:
Power $P$ supplied to a rotating body is given by the product of torque $\tau$ and angular velocity $\omega$.

$P = \tau \omega$

The torque $\tau$ acting on the body is related to its moment of inertia $I$ and angular acceleration $\alpha$ by the relation:

$\tau = I \alpha$

Substituting the value of $\tau$ in the power equation:

$P = (I \alpha) \omega$

Rearranging for instantaneous angular velocity $\omega$:

$\omega = \dfrac{P}{I \alpha}$

Answer: $\dfrac{P}{I\alpha}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A thin uniform rod of length $2$ m cross-sectional area 'A' and density 'd' is rotated about an axis passing through the centre and perpendicular to its length with angular velocity $\omega$. If the value of $\omega$ in terms of its rotational kinetic energy $E$ is $(\alpha E/Ad)^{1/2}$, then the value of $\alpha$ is
questions.solution:
Mass of the rod, $M = \text{Volume} \times \text{density} = A \times L \times d$

Given $L = 2$, $M = 2Ad$

Moment of inertia of the rod about an axis passing through its centre and perpendicular to its length is $I = \dfrac{ML^2}{12}$

Substituting the values of $M$ and $L$, we get $I = \dfrac{2Ad \times 2^2}{12} = \dfrac{2Ad}{3}$

Rotational kinetic energy is given by $E = \dfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2$

Substituting the value of $I$, $E = \dfrac{1}{2} \left( \dfrac{2Ad}{3} \right) \omega^2 = \dfrac{Ad}{3} \omega^2$

Rearranging for $\omega$, we get $\omega = \left( \dfrac{3E}{Ad} \right)^{1/2}$

Comparing this with the given expression $\omega = \left( \dfrac{\alpha E}{Ad} \right)^{1/2}$, we find $\alpha = 3$.

Answer: $3$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Moment of inertia of a disc of mass $M$ and radius 'R' about any of its diameter is $MR^2/4$. The moment of inertia of this disc about an axis normal to the disc and passing through a point on its edge will be, $(x/2) MR^2$. The value of $x$ is
questions.solution:
Given the moment of inertia of the disc about its diameter is $I_{d} = \dfrac{MR^2}{4}$.

By the perpendicular axis theorem, the moment of inertia of the disc about an axis passing through its center and perpendicular to its plane is $I_{c} = I_{d} + I_{d} = \dfrac{MR^2}{4} + \dfrac{MR^2}{4} = \dfrac{MR^2}{2}$.

By the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia of the disc about an axis perpendicular to its plane and passing through a point on its edge is $I = I_{c} + MR^2$.

Substituting the value of $I_{c}$, we get $I = \dfrac{MR^2}{2} + MR^2 = \dfrac{3}{2}MR^2$.

Comparing this with the given expression $\dfrac{x}{2}MR^2$, we get $x = 3$.

Answer: $3$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solid sphere of mass $1$ kg rolls without slipping on a plane surface. Its kinetic energy is $7 \times 10^{-3}$ J. The speed of the center of mass of the sphere in cm s$^{-1}$ is
questions.solution:
Total kinetic energy of a solid sphere rolling without slipping is the sum of its translational and rotational kinetic energies.

$K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2$

For a solid sphere, $I = \dfrac{2}{5}mr^2$ and for pure rolling, $\omega = \dfrac{v}{r}$.

$K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{2}{5}mr^2\right)\left(\dfrac{v}{r}\right)^2$

$K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \dfrac{1}{5}mv^2 = \dfrac{7}{10}mv^2$

Given $K = 7 \times 10^{-3}$ J and $m = 1$ kg.

$7 \times 10^{-3} = \dfrac{7}{10} \times 1 \times v^2$

$v^2 = 10^{-2}$

$v = 0.1$ m s$^{-1}$

$v = 10$ cm s$^{-1}$

Answer: $10$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A disc of radius 0.4 m and mass 1 kg rotates about an axis passing through its centre and perpendicular to its plane. The angular acceleration is 10 rad/s$^2$. The tangential force applied to the rim of the disc is
questions.solution:
The moment of inertia of a disc about an axis passing through its centre and perpendicular to its plane is given by

$I = \dfrac{1}{2}MR^2$

The torque acting on the disc is related to the angular acceleration by

$\tau = I\alpha$

Since the torque is provided by a tangential force $F$ applied at the rim, we have

$\tau = F \times R$

Equating the two expressions for torque:

$F \times R = \dfrac{1}{2}MR^2\alpha$

$F = \dfrac{1}{2}MR\alpha$

Substituting the given values ($M = 1$ kg, $R = 0.4$ m, $\alpha = 10$ rad/s$^2$):

$F = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 1 \times 0.4 \times 10$

$F = 2$ N

Answer: $2$ N

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The relative angular speed of hour hand and minute hand of clock is
questions.solution:
The angular speed of the minute hand is the angle covered in one revolution divided by the time taken (1 hour = 3600 s):

$\omega_m = \dfrac{2\pi}{3600} = \dfrac{\pi}{1800}$ rad/s

The angular speed of the hour hand is the angle covered in one revolution divided by the time taken (12 hours = $12 \times 3600$ s = 43200 s):

$\omega_h = \dfrac{2\pi}{43200} = \dfrac{\pi}{21600}$ rad/s

The relative angular speed of the minute hand with respect to the hour hand is the difference between their angular speeds:

$\omega_{rel} = \omega_m - \omega_h$

$\omega_{rel} = \dfrac{\pi}{1800} - \dfrac{\pi}{21600}$

$\omega_{rel} = \dfrac{12\pi - \pi}{21600} = \dfrac{11\pi}{21600}$ rad/s

Answer: $\dfrac{11\pi}{21600}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body slides down a smooth inclined plane of inclination $\theta$ and reaches the bottom with velocity 'V'. If the same body is a ring which rolls down the same inclined plane then linear velocity at the bottom of the plane is
questions.solution:
Let the height of the inclined plane be $h$.

For the body sliding down the smooth inclined plane, the conservation of mechanical energy gives:

$mgh = \dfrac{1}{2}mV^2$

$V = \sqrt{2gh}$

For the ring rolling down the same inclined plane, the total kinetic energy at the bottom is the sum of translational and rotational kinetic energy:

$mgh = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2$

For a ring, the moment of inertia is $I = mR^2$ and for pure rolling, $\omega = \dfrac{v}{R}$. Substituting these values:

$mgh = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}(mR^2)\left(\dfrac{v}{R}\right)^2$

$mgh = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = mv^2$

$v = \sqrt{gh}$

Comparing the two velocities:

$v = \dfrac{\sqrt{2gh}}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{V}{\sqrt{2}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Let M and L be the mass and length of thin uniform rod respectively. In first case, axis of rotation is passing through centre and perpendicular to length of rod. In second case axis of rotation is passing through one end and perpendicular to length of rod. The ratio of radius of gyration in first case to second case is
questions.solution:
Moment of inertia of a thin uniform rod about an axis passing through its centre and perpendicular to its length is $I_1 = \dfrac{ML^2}{12}$.

Radius of gyration in the first case is $K_1 = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_1}{M}} = \dfrac{L}{\sqrt{12}}$.

Moment of inertia of the rod about an axis passing through one end and perpendicular to its length is $I_2 = \dfrac{ML^2}{3}$.

Radius of gyration in the second case is $K_2 = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_2}{M}} = \dfrac{L}{\sqrt{3}}$.

The ratio of radius of gyration in the first case to the second case is $\dfrac{K_1}{K_2} = \dfrac{\dfrac{L}{\sqrt{12}}}{\dfrac{L}{\sqrt{3}}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3}{12}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{4}} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The moment of inertia of a ring about an axis passing through its centre and perpendicular to its plane is I. It is rotating with angular velocity $\omega$. Another identical ring is gently placed on it so that their centres coincide. If both rings are rotating about the same axis then loss in kinetic energy is
questions.solution:
Initial angular momentum of the system is $L_i = I\omega$

Initial kinetic energy is $K_i = \dfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2$

When an identical ring is placed on it, the new moment of inertia becomes $I_f = I + I = 2I$

By conservation of angular momentum, $I_f\omega_f = I_i\omega_i$

$2I\omega_f = I\omega \Rightarrow \omega_f = \dfrac{\omega}{2}$

Final kinetic energy is $K_f = \dfrac{1}{2}(2I)\left(\dfrac{\omega}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{4}I\omega^2$

Loss in kinetic energy is $\Delta K = K_i - K_f = \dfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2 - \dfrac{1}{4}I\omega^2 = \dfrac{I\omega^2}{4}$

Answer: $\dfrac{I\omega^2}{4}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A flywheel rotating about a fixed axis has a kinetic energy of $500$ joule, if its angular frequency is $5$ Hz, then calculate the moment of inertia of the wheel about the axis of rotation. ($\pi^2=10$)
questions.solution:
Given kinetic energy $K = 500$ J and angular frequency $f = 5$ Hz.

Angular velocity $\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi \times 5 = 10\pi$ rad/s.

The rotational kinetic energy is given by $K = \dfrac{1}{2} I \omega^2$.

Substituting the values:

$500 = \dfrac{1}{2} I (10\pi)^2$

$500 = \dfrac{1}{2} I (100\pi^2)$

Given $\pi^2 = 10$:

$500 = \dfrac{1}{2} I (100 \times 10)$

$500 = 500 I$

$I = 1 \text{ kg m}^2$

Answer: $1 \text{ kg m}^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A wheel is rotating at $600$ rpm about its axis of rotation. When the power is cut off, it comes to rest in half a minute. Its angular retardation expressed in $\text{rad}/\text{s}^2$ is (retardation is uniform)
questions.solution:
Initial angular velocity, $\omega_0 = 600 \text{ rpm} = \dfrac{600 \times 2\pi}{60} \text{ rad/s} = 20\pi \text{ rad/s}$

Final angular velocity, $\omega = 0$

Time taken to come to rest, $t = 30 \text{ s}$

Using the equation of kinematics for rotational motion, $\omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t$

$0 = 20\pi + \alpha (30)$

$\alpha = -\dfrac{2\pi}{3} \text{ rad/s}^2$

The angular retardation is $\dfrac{2\pi}{3} \text{ rad/s}^2$.

Answer: $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The angular momentum of a rotating body is ' $L$ '. When the frequency of rotating body is tripled and its kinetic energy is made one-third, the new angular momentum becomes
questions.solution:
The angular momentum $L$ and rotational kinetic energy $K$ of a rotating body are related by its angular velocity $\omega = 2\pi f$, where $f$ is the frequency. Starting from the definition of rotational kinetic energy, $K = \frac{1}{2} I \omega^2$, and substituting the angular momentum relation $L = I \omega$ to eliminate the moment of inertia $I$, we obtain $I = \frac{L}{\omega}$.

Substituting into the kinetic energy expression gives $K = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{L}{\omega} \cdot \omega^2 = \frac{1}{2} L \omega$. Replacing $\omega$ with $2\pi f$ yields $K = \frac{1}{2} L (2\pi f) = \pi L f$, which rearranges to $L = \frac{K}{\pi f}$.

For the initial state, $L_1 = \frac{K_1}{\pi f_1}$. When the frequency is tripled to $f_2 = 3f_1$ and the kinetic energy is reduced to one-third, $K_2 = \frac{1}{3} K_1$, the new angular momentum becomes $L_2 = \frac{K_2}{\pi f_2} = \frac{\frac{1}{3} K_1}{\pi (3f_1)} = \frac{1}{9} \cdot \frac{K_1}{\pi f_1} = \frac{1}{9} L_1$.

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{A}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The moment of inertia of a thin uniform rod of mass ' $M$ ' and length ' $L$ ', about an axis perpendicular to length of the rod and at a distance ' $\mathrm{L} / 4$ ' from one end is
questions.solution:
Moment of inertia via parallel axis theorem:

The moment of inertia about the center of mass axis is $I_{\text{CM}} = \frac{ML^2}{12}$.

The distance from the given axis to the center of mass is $d = |\frac{L}{2} - \frac{L}{4}| = \frac{L}{4}$.

Applying the parallel axis theorem $I = I_{\text{CM}} + Md^2$:

$I = \frac{ML^2}{12} + M\left(\frac{L}{4}\right)^2 = \frac{ML^2}{12} + \frac{ML^2}{16}$

Combining terms with common denominator 48:

$I = \frac{4ML^2}{48} + \frac{3ML^2}{48} = \frac{7ML^2}{48}$

Final moment of inertia: $\frac{7ML^2}{48}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Four particles each of mass ' m ' are lying symmetrically on the rim of disc of mass ' $M$ ' and radius ' $R$ '. Moment of inertia of the system about an axis passing through one of the particle and perpendicular to plane of disc is
questions.solution:
Moment of inertia of the system

The axis passes through particle P1 and is perpendicular to the disc plane. The disc’s moment of inertia about this axis, via the parallel axis theorem, is $I_{\text{disc}} = \frac{1}{2}MR^2 + MR^2 = \frac{3}{2}MR^2$.

For the four particles on the rim: P1 lies on the axis ($r_1 = 0$), P2 and P4 are each at distance $R\sqrt{2}$ ($I = 2mR^2$), and P3 is diametrically opposite ($r_3 = 2R$, $I = 4mR^2$). Their total moment of inertia is $I_{\text{particles}} = 0 + 2mR^2 + 4mR^2 + 2mR^2 = 8mR^2$.

The system’s total moment of inertia is therefore

$I_{\text{total}} = \frac{3}{2}MR^2 + 8mR^2 = \frac{(3M + 16m)R^2}{2}$

This corresponds to option B.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A thin wire of length ' $L$ ' and uniform linear mass density ' $\lambda$ ' is bent into a circular ring. The moment of inertia of ring about a tangential axis in its plane is
questions.solution:
Given a wire of length $L$ with uniform linear mass density $\lambda$, the total mass is $M = \lambda L$.

When formed into a circular ring, the circumference equals the wire length, so $L = 2\pi R$ and $R = \frac{L}{2\pi}$.

The moment of inertia about a diameter is $I_d = \frac{MR^2}{2}$ by the perpendicular axis theorem.

Applying the parallel axis theorem for a tangential axis in the plane, located distance $R$ from the center:

$I_{\text{tangential}} = I_d + MR^2 = \frac{MR^2}{2} + MR^2 = \frac{3}{2}MR^2$.

Substituting $M = \lambda L$ and $R = \frac{L}{2\pi}$:

$I_{\text{tangential}} = \frac{3}{2}(\lambda L)\left(\frac{L}{2\pi}\right)^2 = \frac{3\lambda L^3}{8\pi^2}$.

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{C}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solid sphere is in purely rotational motion about its diameter. The ratio of its angular momentum and kinetic energy is $\frac{\pi}{22}$. Find angular velocity of the sphere. ( $\pi=22 / 7$ )
questions.solution:
Angular momentum and rotational kinetic energy relate through the moment of inertia $I = \frac{2}{5}MR^2$ and angular velocity $\omega$ as $L = I\omega$ and $K = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$ respectively.

The ratio simplifies to $\frac{L}{K} = \frac{I\omega}{\frac{1}{2}I\omega^2} = \frac{2}{\omega}$.
Given $\frac{L}{K} = \frac{\pi}{22}$, we equate $\frac{2}{\omega} = \frac{\pi}{22}$.

Solving for angular velocity: $\omega = \frac{44}{\pi}$.

Substituting $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$ yields $\omega = 44 \times \frac{7}{22} = 14$ rad/s.

The angular velocity is therefore $14$ rad/s.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A same torque is applied to a disc and a ring of equal mass and radii then
options: the ring will rotate with greater angular frequency.
both will rotate with same angular frequency.
the disc will rotate with greater angular frequency.
both will rotate with same angular velocity.
questions.solution:
Rotational dynamics analysis shows that for a constant applied torque $\tau$, the angular acceleration $\alpha$ relates to moment of inertia $I$ through $\tau = I\alpha$.

For identical mass and radius, a disc has $I_{\text{disc}} = \frac{1}{2}MR^2$ while a ring has $I_{\text{ring}} = MR^2$, establishing $I_{\text{ring}} = 2I_{\text{disc}}$.

With $\tau$ constant, $I\alpha$ remains equal for both objects. Since $I_{\text{ring}} \gt I_{\text{disc}}$, it follows that $\alpha_{\text{disc}} \gt \alpha_{\text{ring}}$. From the inertia ratio, $\alpha_{\text{disc}} = 2\alpha_{\text{ring}}$.

Starting from rest, angular frequency evolves as $\omega = \alpha t$. The disc's greater angular acceleration produces higher angular frequency over any duration $t$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solid sphere at rests rolls down an inclined plane of vertical height $h$ without sliding. Its speed on reaching the bottom of plane is ($g=$ acceleration due to gravity)
questions.solution:
Applying conservation of mechanical energy for the solid sphere rolling without slipping down the inclined plane, the initial potential energy $mgh$ converts to both translational and rotational kinetic energy at the bottom.

For a solid sphere, $I = \frac{2}{5}mr^2$ and $\omega = v/r$. The rotational kinetic energy becomes $\frac{1}{2}I\omega^2 = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{2}{5}mr^2 \cdot \frac{v^2}{r^2} = \frac{1}{5}mv^2$.

The total kinetic energy is then $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 + \frac{1}{5}mv^2 = \frac{7}{10}mv^2$.

Equating $mgh = \frac{7}{10}mv^2$ and solving for velocity yields $v = \sqrt{\frac{10gh}{7}}$.

$\boxed{\left(\frac{10 g h}{7}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A man standing on a turn-table is rotating at a certain angular frequency with his arms outstretched. He suddenly folds his arms. If his moment of inertia with folded arms is $75 \%$ of that with outstretched arms, then his rotational kinetic energy will
questions.solution:
Let $I_1$ and $\omega_1$ represent the initial moment of inertia and angular velocity, with $I_2$ and $\omega_2$ the final values after the man folds his arms. The moment of inertia decreases to $I_2 = \frac{3}{4}I_1$.

Angular momentum conservation gives $I_1\omega_1 = I_2\omega_2$. Substituting yields $I_1\omega_1 = \frac{3}{4}I_1\omega_2$, so $\omega_2 = \frac{4}{3}\omega_1$.

The rotational kinetic energy increases from $KE_1 = \frac{1}{2}I_1\omega_1^2$ to $KE_2 = \frac{1}{2}I_2\omega_2^2 = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{3}{4}I_1\right)\left(\frac{4}{3}\omega_1\right)^2 = \frac{1}{2}I_1\omega_1^2 \cdot \frac{4}{3} = \frac{4}{3}KE_1$.

The kinetic energy increases by $\Delta KE = KE_2 - KE_1 = \frac{1}{3}KE_1$, representing a $\frac{1}{3} \times 100\% \approx 33.3\%$ increase.

The rotational kinetic energy increases by approximately $33.3\%$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A rigid body rotates about a fixed axis with variable angular velocity ($\propto-\beta \mathrm{t}$) at time t, where $\propto$ and $\beta$ are constants. The angle through which it rotates before it comes to rest is
questions.solution:
The angular velocity is $\omega = \alpha - \beta t$. The body reaches rest when $\omega = 0$, giving $\alpha - \beta t_f = 0$ and $t_f = \frac{\alpha}{\beta}$.

The total rotation angle is the integral of angular velocity over time:

$\theta = \int_0^{\alpha/\beta} (\alpha - \beta t) \, dt = \left[ \alpha t - \frac{\beta t^2}{2} \right]_0^{\alpha/\beta}$

Evaluating at the limits:

$\theta = \left( \alpha \cdot \frac{\alpha}{\beta} - \frac{\beta}{2} \cdot \frac{\alpha^2}{\beta^2} \right) - 0 = \frac{\alpha^2}{\beta} - \frac{\alpha^2}{2\beta} = \frac{\alpha^2}{2\beta}$

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{C}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Moment of inertia of a solid sphere about its diameter is 'I'. It is then casted into 27 small spheres of same diameter. The moment of inertia of each small sphere about its diameter is
questions.solution:
Given a solid sphere of mass $M$ and radius $R$ with moment of inertia $I = \frac{2}{5} M R^2$ about its diameter.

When recast into 27 smaller spheres of equal diameter, mass conservation gives $M = 27m$, so $m = \frac{M}{27}$.

Volume conservation implies $\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = 27 \times \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$, leading to $R^3 = 27r^3$ and $r = \frac{R}{3}$.

Each small sphere has moment of inertia $I' = \frac{2}{5} m r^2$.
Substituting $m = \frac{M}{27}$ and $r = \frac{R}{3}$,
this becomes $I' = \frac{2}{5} \left(\frac{M}{27}\right) \left(\frac{R}{3}\right)^2 = \frac{2}{5} M R^2 \times \frac{1}{243}$.

Recognizing $\frac{2}{5} M R^2 = I$, we obtain $I' = \frac{I}{243}$.

The moment of inertia of each small sphere about its diameter is $\frac{I}{243}$.

The correct answer is $\boxed{\text{D}}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Moment of inertia of the rod about an axis passing through the centre and perpendicular to its length is ' $\mathrm{I}_1$ '. The same rod is bent into a ring and its moment of inertia about the diameter is ' $I_2$ '. Then $I_1 / I_2$ is
questions.solution:
The moment of inertia for a rod of mass $M$ and length $L$ about its center perpendicular axis is $I_1 = \frac{1}{12} M L^2$.

When bent into a ring, the circumference becomes $L = 2\pi R$, giving radius $R = \frac{L}{2\pi}$. The moment of inertia for a ring about its diameter is $I_2 = \frac{1}{2} M R^2 = \frac{1}{2} M \left(\frac{L}{2\pi}\right)^2 = \frac{M L^2}{8\pi^2}$.

The ratio is $\frac{I_1}{I_2} = \frac{\frac{1}{12} M L^2}{\frac{1}{8\pi^2} M L^2} = \frac{8\pi^2}{12} = \frac{2\pi^2}{3}$, matching option B.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A bob of mass ' m ' is tied by a massless string whose other end is wound on a flywheel (disc) of radius ' $R$ ' and mass ' $m$ '. When released from the rest, the bob starts falling vertically downwards. If the bob has covered a vertical distance ' $h$ ', then angular speed of wheel will be (There is no slipping between string and wheel, $g$ - acceleration due to gravity)
questions.solution:
Conservation of mechanical energy is applied to the system, taking the initial state when the bob is at rest and the final state after it has fallen distance $h$.

Initial potential energy is $mgh$, with zero kinetic energy for both bob and flywheel. Final energy consists of translational kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ for the bob and rotational kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$ for the flywheel.

For a solid disc, $I = \frac{1}{2}mR^2$. The no-slip condition gives $v = R\omega$.

Equating initial and final energies:

$mgh = \frac{1}{2}m(R\omega)^2 + \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{2}mR^2\right)\omega^2$

Simplifying yields:

$mgh = \frac{3}{4}mR^2\omega^2$

Solving for $\omega$:

$\omega^2 = \frac{4gh}{3R^2}$

$\omega = \frac{2}{R}\sqrt{\frac{gh}{3}}$

This corresponds to option A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A thin uniform rod of length ' $L$ ' and mass ' $M$ ' is swinging freely about a horizontal axis passing through its end. Its maximum angular speed is ' $\omega$ '. Its centre of mass rises to a maximum height of ( $g=$ acceleration due gravity)
questions.solution:
Maximum height of center of mass using conservation of mechanical energy

The lowest position serves as the reference level for potential energy, so $\text{PE}_{\text{initial}} = 0$.

At maximum angular speed $\omega$, the kinetic energy is purely rotational: $\text{KE}_{\text{initial}} = \frac{1}{2} I \omega^2$.

For a thin uniform rod of length $L$ and mass $M$ rotating about its end, the moment of inertia is $I = \frac{1}{3} M L^2$, yielding $\text{KE}_{\text{initial}} = \frac{1}{6} M L^2 \omega^2$.

At the highest point, angular speed is zero: $\text{KE}_{\text{final}} = 0$ and $\text{PE}_{\text{final}} = M g h$.

By conservation of mechanical energy: $\frac{1}{6} M L^2 \omega^2 = M g h$.

Solving for $h$: $h = \frac{L^2 \omega^2}{6 g}$.

The result matches option D.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The moment of inertia of a solid sphere of mass ' $m$ ' and radius ' $R$ ' about its diametric axis is 'I'. Its moment of inertia about a tangent in the plane is
questions.solution:
Moment of inertia about diameter: $I = \frac{2}{5} mR^2$

Using the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia about a tangent in the same plane is $I_{\text{tangent}} = I + mR^2$. Substituting $mR^2 = \frac{5}{2}I$ from the first expression gives $I_{\text{tangent}} = I + \frac{5}{2}I = \frac{7}{2}I$.

The moment of inertia about the tangent is therefore $3.5$ times that about the diameter, matching option C.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two discs of moment of inertia ' $\mathrm{I}_1$ ' and ' $\mathrm{I}_2$ ' and angular speeds ' $\omega_1{ }^{\prime}$ and ' $\omega_2$ ' are rotating along the collinear axes passing through their centre of mass and perpendicular to their plane. If the two discs are made to rotate together along the same axis. The rotational kinetic energy of the system will be
questions.solution:
Conservation of angular momentum applies since no external torques act on the system.

The initial angular momentum is $L_i = I_1 \omega_1 + I_2 \omega_2$.

When rotating together, the combined moment of inertia becomes $I_f = I_1 + I_2$ with common angular speed $\omega_f$. The final angular momentum is $L_f = (I_1 + I_2)\omega_f$.

Equating $L_i = L_f$ gives:

$I_1 \omega_1 + I_2 \omega_2 = (I_1 + I_2)\omega_f$

Solving for $\omega_f$:

$\omega_f = \frac{I_1 \omega_1 + I_2 \omega_2}{I_1 + I_2}$

The final kinetic energy is:

$K_f = \frac{1}{2}(I_1 + I_2)\omega_f^2 = \frac{1}{2}(I_1 + I_2) \left( \frac{I_1 \omega_1 + I_2 \omega_2}{I_1 + I_2} \right)^2$

Simplifying:

$K_f = \frac{(I_1 \omega_1 + I_2 \omega_2)^2}{2(I_1 + I_2)}$

This matches option D.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Four particles each of mass $M$ are placed at the corners of a square of side L. The radius of gyration of the system about an axis perpendicular to the square and passing through its centre is
questions.solution:
The axis of rotation passes perpendicularly through the center of the square with side length $L$. Each particle of mass $M$ lies at distance $r = L/\sqrt{2}$ from the center, equal to half the diagonal length.

The moment of inertia for one particle is $Mr^2 = M(L/\sqrt{2})^2 = ML^2/2$. For four identical particles, the total moment of inertia becomes $I_{\text{total}} = 4 \times (ML^2/2) = 2ML^2$.

Using the relationship $I_{\text{total}} = (4M)K^2$ for the system’s total mass $4M$ and radius of gyration $K$, we substitute $2ML^2 = 4MK^2$.

Solving yields $K^2 = L^2/2$, so $K = L/\sqrt{2}$.

The radius of gyration is $\boxed{\text{B}}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: What is the linear velocity if angular velocity $\vec{\omega}=3 \hat{i}-4 \hat{j}+\hat{k}$ and radius $\vec{r}=(5 \hat{i}-6 \hat{j}+6 \hat{k})$ ?
questions.solution:
The linear velocity is obtained from the cross product $\vec{v} = \vec{\omega} \times \vec{r}$ where $\vec{\omega} = 3\hat{i} - 4\hat{j} + \hat{k}$ and $\vec{r} = 5\hat{i} - 6\hat{j} + 6\hat{k}$.

Computing the determinant:

$\vec{v} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 3 & -4 & 1 \\ 5 & -6 & 6 \end{vmatrix} = \hat{i}(-24 + 6) - \hat{j}(18 - 5) + \hat{k}(-18 + 20) = -18\hat{i} - 13\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$

This result corresponds to option C.

$\boxed{\text{C}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A thin metal wire of length ' $L$ ' and mass ' $M$ ' is bent to form semicircular ring as shown. The moment of inertia about $\mathrm{XX}^1$ is
questions.solution:
The moment of inertia about a diameter of a semicircular ring of mass $M$ and length $L$ requires relating the geometric parameters. For a semicircle of radius $R$, the arc length gives $L = \pi R$, so $R = L / \pi$.

The moment of inertia about diameter $XX'$ is derived by integration. A mass element $dm = (M / \pi) d\theta$ at angle $\theta$ has perpendicular distance $R \sin \theta$ from the axis, contributing $dI = dm \cdot (R \sin \theta)^2 = (M R^2 / \pi) \sin^2 \theta d\theta$.

Integrating from $0$ to $\pi$:

$I = \frac{M R^2}{\pi} \int_0^\pi \sin^2 \theta d\theta = \frac{M R^2}{\pi} \int_0^\pi \frac{1 - \cos 2\theta}{2} d\theta = \frac{M R^2}{2\pi} \left[ \theta - \frac{\sin 2\theta}{2} \right]_0^\pi = \frac{M R^2}{2}$

Substituting $R = L / \pi$ yields:

$I = \frac{M}{2} \left( \frac{L}{\pi} \right)^2 = \frac{M L^2}{2\pi^2}$

Final answer: $\frac{M L^2}{2\pi^2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solid cylinder of mass ' M ' and radius ' R ' is rotating about its geometrical axis. A solid sphere of same mass and same radius is also rotating about its diameter with an angular speed half that of the cylinder. The ratio of the kinetic energy of rotation of the sphere to that of the cylinder will be
questions.solution:
Kinetic energy ratio calculation

Given a solid cylinder and solid sphere with equal mass $M$ and radius $R$, where the cylinder rotates with angular speed $\omega$ and the sphere with $\omega/2$. The rotational kinetic energy ratio $\frac{K_s}{K_c}$ is determined.

The moment of inertia for the cylinder about its axis is $I_c = \frac{1}{2}MR^2$, yielding kinetic energy $K_c = \frac{1}{2}I_c\omega^2 = \frac{1}{4}MR^2\omega^2$.

For the sphere about its diameter, $I_s = \frac{2}{5}MR^2$, with kinetic energy $K_s = \frac{1}{2}I_s(\omega/2)^2 = \frac{1}{20}MR^2\omega^2$.

The ratio simplifies as follows:

$\frac{K_s}{K_c} = \frac{\frac{1}{20}MR^2\omega^2}{\frac{1}{4}MR^2\omega^2} = \frac{1}{5}$

The kinetic energy ratio of sphere to cylinder is $1:5$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solid sphere of mass ' m ' and radius ' R ' is rotating about its diameter. A solid cylinder of the same mass and same radius is also rotating about its geometrical axis with angular speed twice that of sphere. The ratio of kinetic energy of sphere to kinetic energy of cylinder will be
questions.solution:
Given a solid sphere and solid cylinder with equal mass $m$ and radius $R$, rotating about their respective axes with angular speeds $\omega_c = 2\omega_s$.

The moment of inertia for a solid sphere is $I_s = \frac{2}{5}mR^2$, yielding rotational kinetic energy $KE_s = \frac{1}{2}I_s\omega_s^2 = \frac{1}{5}mR^2\omega_s^2$.

For the solid cylinder, $I_c = \frac{1}{2}mR^2$, and with $\omega_c = 2\omega_s$, its kinetic energy becomes $KE_c = \frac{1}{2}I_c\omega_c^2 = mR^2\omega_s^2$.

The ratio is therefore $\frac{KE_s}{KE_c} = \frac{\frac{1}{5}mR^2\omega_s^2}{mR^2\omega_s^2} = \frac{1}{5}$.

Answer: $\boxed{B}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A solid sphere and thin walled hollow sphere have same mass and same material. Which of them have greater moment of inertia about their diameter?
[ $\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{h}}=$ moment of inertia of hollow sphere about an axis coinciding with its diameter, $\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{s}}=$ moment of inertia of solid sphere about an axis coinciding with its diameter]
questions.solution:
The moment of inertia depends on both the mass and its distribution relative to the rotation axis. For a solid sphere of mass $M$ and radius $R$, the moment of inertia about a diameter is $I_s = \frac{2}{5}MR^2$.

For a thin-walled hollow sphere of equal mass and radius, the moment of inertia is $I_h = \frac{2}{3}MR^2$.

Since the mass in the hollow sphere is concentrated entirely at its outer surface, it is distributed farther from the axis of rotation. The coefficients confirm this relationship: $\frac{2}{3} \gt \frac{2}{5}$, so $I_h \gt I_s$.

The hollow sphere has greater moment of inertia.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The moment of inertia of a ring about an axis passing through its centre and perpendicular to its plane is I. It is rotating with angular velocity $\omega$. Another identical ring is gently placed on it so that their centres coincide. If both the rings are rotating about the same axis then loss in kinetic energy is
questions.solution:
The moment of inertia $I$ and initial angular velocity $\omega$ characterize the first ring. The system's initial angular momentum is conserved since no external torque acts upon it. The initial angular momentum is $L_i = I\omega$.

When a second identical ring is placed concentrically, the total moment of inertia becomes $I_f = I + I = 2I$. Conservation of angular momentum gives $I\omega = 2I\omega_f$, so the final angular velocity is $\omega_f = \omega / 2$.

The initial kinetic energy is $KE_i = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$. The final kinetic energy is $KE_f = \frac{1}{2}(2I)(\omega/2)^2 = \frac{1}{4}I\omega^2$.

The kinetic energy loss is $\Delta KE = KE_i - KE_f = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2 - \frac{1}{4}I\omega^2 = \frac{1}{4}I\omega^2$.

Final answer: $\boxed{C}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body is rotating about its own axis. Its rotational kinetic energy is ' $x$ ' and its angular momentum is ' y '. Hence its moment of inertia about its own axis is
questions.solution:
Rotational kinetic energy and angular momentum are defined by the equations $K = \frac{1}{2} I \omega^2$ and $L = I \omega$, respectively.

Solving the angular momentum equation for $\omega$ yields $\omega = \frac{L}{I}$.

Substituting this into the energy equation gives $K = \frac{1}{2} I \left(\frac{L}{I}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{L^2}{I}$.

Rearranging for moment of inertia results in $I = \frac{L^2}{2K}$.

Using the given values $K = x$ and $L = y$ produces $I = \frac{y^2}{2x}$, which corresponds to option B.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Moment of inertia of a thin uniform rod rotating about the perpendicular axis passing through its centre is 'I'. If the same rod is bent in the form of ring, its moment of inertia about the diameter is ' $\mathrm{I}_1{ }^{\prime}$. If $I_1=x I$, then the value of ' $x$ ' is
questions.solution:
The moment of inertia of a thin uniform rod about its center is $I = \frac{1}{12}ML^2$.

When bent into a ring of radius $R$, the circumference equals the rod length: $L = 2\pi R$, so $R = \frac{L}{2\pi}$. The moment of inertia about a diameter becomes $I_1 = \frac{1}{2}MR^2 = \frac{1}{2}M\left(\frac{L}{2\pi}\right)^2 = \frac{ML^2}{8\pi^2}$.

With $I_1 = xI$, we substitute: $\frac{ML^2}{8\pi^2} = x\left(\frac{1}{12}ML^2\right)$. Canceling $ML^2$ yields $\frac{1}{8\pi^2} = \frac{x}{12}$, so $x = \frac{12}{8\pi^2} = \frac{3}{2\pi^2}$.

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{B}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A disc of mass 25 kg and radius 0.2 m is rotating at 240 r.p.m. A retarding torque brings it to rest in 20 second. If the torque is due to a force applied tangentially on the rim of the disc then the magnitude of the force is
questions.solution:
The initial angular speed is $\omega_0 = 240 \times \frac{2\pi}{60} = 8\pi \text{rad/s}$, and the disc comes to rest so $\omega = 0$.

Using $\omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t$ with $t = 20\text{s}$ gives $0 = 8\pi + 20\alpha$, leading to $\alpha = -\frac{2\pi}{5}\text{rad/s}^2$, with magnitude $|\alpha| = \frac{2\pi}{5}\text{rad/s}^2$.

The moment of inertia is $I = \frac{1}{2}MR^2 = \frac{1}{2}(25)(0.2)^2 = 0.5\text{kg m}^2$.

The torque is $\tau = I|\alpha| = 0.5 \times \frac{2\pi}{5} = \frac{\pi}{5}\text{N m}$.

Since $\tau = FR$, the force magnitude is $F = \frac{\pi/5}{0.2} = \pi\text{N}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two circular loops P and Q of radii 'r' and 'nr' are made respectively from a uniform wire. Moment of inertia of loop Q about its axis is 4 times that of loop P about its axis. The value of n is
questions.solution:
Linear mass density $\lambda$ is constant for both loops. The mass of each loop equals $\lambda$ times its circumference.

For loop P with radius $r$, mass $M_P = \lambda \cdot 2\pi r$ and moment of inertia about its axis $I_P = M_P r^2 = 2\pi\lambda r^3$.

For loop Q with radius $nr$, mass $M_Q = \lambda \cdot 2\pi nr$ and moment of inertia $I_Q = M_Q (nr)^2 = 2\pi\lambda n^3 r^3$.

Given $I_Q = 4I_P$, substituting yields $2\pi\lambda n^3 r^3 = 4(2\pi\lambda r^3)$.

Canceling $2\pi\lambda r^3$ from both sides gives $n^3 = 4$, so $n = 4^{1/3} = (2^2)^{1/3} = 2^{2/3}$.

The value $n = 2^{2/3}$ corresponds to option B.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Three spheres, each of mass ' $m$ ' and radius ' $r$ ' are placed as shown in figure. Consider an axis $\mathrm{YY}^1$, which is touching two spheres and passing through the diameter of third sphere. The moment of inertia of the system consisting of these three spheres about $\mathrm{YY}^1$ axis is
questions.solution:
Moment of inertia of Sphere 1: Since axis $\mathrm{YY}^1$ passes through its diameter, $I_1 = \frac{2}{5}mr^2$.

Moment of inertia of Sphere 2 and Sphere 3: The axis is tangential to both spheres at distance $r$ from their centers. Using the parallel axis theorem, $I_2 = I_3 = \frac{2}{5}mr^2 + mr^2 = \frac{7}{5}mr^2$.

Summing the contributions: $I_{\text{total}} = I_1 + I_2 + I_3 = \frac{2}{5}mr^2 + \frac{7}{5}mr^2 + \frac{7}{5}mr^2 = \frac{16}{5}mr^2$.

The result corresponds to option C.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A wheel initially at rest, begins to rotate about its axis with constant angular acceleration. If it rotates through an angle $\theta_1$ in first 2 s and a further angle $\theta_2$ in the next 2 s , the ratio $\theta_1: \theta_2$ is
questions.solution:
For a wheel rotating with constant angular acceleration α starting from rest, the angular displacement follows θ = (1/2)αt2.

During the first 2 seconds: θ1 = (1/2)α(2)2 = 2α

During the first 4 seconds: θtotal = (1/2)α(4)2 = 8α

The angular displacement during the subsequent 2 seconds is therefore θ2 = θtotal - θ1 = 8α - 2α = 6α

The ratio θ1 : θ2 evaluates to 2α : 6α = 1 : 3.

Final answer: D

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solid sphere rolling without friction on a horizontal surface with a constant speed of $2 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$, rolls up on an inclined ramp which is inclined at $30^{\circ}$. The maximum distance travelled by the sphere on the inclined ramp is (acceleration due to gravity $g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2, \sin 30^{\circ}=1 / 2$)
questions.solution:
The mechanical energy is conserved since no friction acts on the system. The total kinetic energy of a rolling sphere without slipping comprises translational and rotational components, with moment of inertia $I = \frac{2}{5}mr^2$ for a solid sphere.

The initial kinetic energy with speed $v = 2\mathrm{m/s}$ is $KE_i = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 + \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$. Substituting $\omega = v/r$ and simplifying yields $KE_i = \frac{7}{10}mv^2$.

At maximum displacement $s$ along the $30^\circ$ incline, the sphere comes to rest. The height gained is $h = s\sin30^\circ = s/2$, so the potential energy becomes $PE_f = mgs/2$.

Energy conservation gives $\frac{7}{10}mv^2 = mgs/2$. Solving for $s$ and using $g = 10\mathrm{m/s^2}$:

$s = \frac{7v^2}{5g} = \frac{7 \times 4}{5 \times 10} = \frac{28}{50} = 0.56\mathrm{m}$

Converting to centimeters: $s = 56\mathrm{cm}$.

Final answer: 56 cm

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A disc of mass ' $m$ ' and radius ' $r$ ' rolls down an inclined plane of height ' h '. When it reaches the bottom of the plane, its rotational kinetic energy is ( $\mathrm{g}=$ acceleration due to gravity)
questions.solution:
The rotational kinetic energy of the disc rolling down the inclined plane without slipping is determined using conservation of mechanical energy.

At height h, the potential energy mgh converts fully to kinetic energy at the bottom, comprising both translational and rotational components: $mgh = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 + \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$.

For a disc, $I = \frac{1}{2}mr^2$. With no slipping, $\omega = v/r$, so the rotational term becomes $\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{2}mr^2 \cdot \left(\frac{v}{r}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{4}mv^2$. Substituting, $mgh = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 + \frac{1}{4}mv^2 = \frac{3}{4}mv^2$.

Solving for $mv^2$ gives $mv^2 = \frac{4}{3}mgh$. Rotational kinetic energy is $KE_r = \frac{1}{4}mv^2 = \frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{4}{3}mgh = \frac{1}{3}mgh$.

Answer: $\frac{1}{3}mgh$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two discs $A$ and $B$ of same material and thickness have radii $R$ and $3 R$ respectively. Their moments of inertia about their axis will be in the ratio
questions.solution:
Key concept: The moment of inertia of a homogeneous disc about its central axis is $I = \frac{1}{2} M R^2$, where mass scales proportionally to the square of the radius for constant thickness and density.

Given $R_B = 3R_A$, it follows from $M \propto R^2$ that $M_B = 9M_A$.

Then for disc A: $I_A = \frac{1}{2} M_A R_A^2$
For disc B: $I_B = \frac{1}{2} (9M_A) (3R_A)^2 = \frac{1}{2} (9M_A)(9R_A^2) = \frac{81}{2} M_A R_A^2$

The ratio is $\frac{I_A}{I_B} = \frac{ \frac{1}{2} M_A R_A^2 }{ \frac{81}{2} M_A R_A^2 } = \frac{1}{81}$

Final answer: $\boxed{C}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An inclined plane makes an angle $30^{\circ}$ with the horizontal. A solid sphere rolling down an inclined plane from rest without slipping has linear acceleration ( $g=$ acceleration due gravity) $\left(\sin 30^{\circ}=0.5\right)$
questions.solution:
Finding the linear acceleration of a solid sphere rolling without slipping requires applying Newton’s second law to both translational and rotational motion. The gravitational force component along the incline is $Mg\sin\theta$, while friction $f_s$ acts up the incline.

The net force equation along the incline is:

$Mg\sin\theta - f_s = Ma$

For rotation about the center, the torque from friction gives:

$f_s R = I\alpha$

The no-slip condition relates linear and angular acceleration: $a = R\alpha$. For a solid sphere, $I = \frac{2}{5}MR^2$. Substituting yields:

$f_s R = \left(\frac{2}{5}MR^2\right)\left(\frac{a}{R}\right)$

which simplifies to $f_s = \frac{2}{5}Ma$.

Inserting this into the force equation:

$Mg\sin\theta - \frac{2}{5}Ma = Ma$

$Mg\sin\theta = \frac{7}{5}Ma$

Solving for acceleration:

$a = \frac{5}{7}g\sin\theta$

For $\theta = 30^\circ$, $\sin\theta = \frac{1}{2}$, so:

$a = \frac{5g}{14}$

The correct choice is B.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two spheres each of mass M and radius R are connected with a massless rod of length 4 R . The moment of inertia of the system about an axis passing through the centre of one of the spheres and perpendicular to the rod will be
questions.solution:
Moment of inertia about an axis through the center of one sphere perpendicular to the rod

The axis passes through the center of the first sphere, making its moment of inertia that of a solid sphere about its diameter: $I_1 = \frac{2}{5}MR^2$.

For the second sphere, apply the parallel axis theorem. The distance between centers is $4R$, since the rod length of $4R$ is interpreted as center-to-center distance. The moment of inertia about the parallel axis is $I_2 = \frac{2}{5}MR^2 + M(4R)^2 = \frac{82}{5}MR^2$.

The total moment of inertia sums contributions from both spheres:
$I_\text{total} = I_1 + I_2 = \frac{2}{5}MR^2 + \frac{82}{5}MR^2 = \frac{84}{5}MR^2$.

This result corresponds to option B.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body slides down a smooth inclined plane of inclination $\theta$ and reaches the bottom with velocity V. If the same body is a ring which rolls down the same inclined plane then linear velocity at the bottom of plane is
questions.solution:
The body of mass $m$ descends from height $h$ on an inclined plane.

For sliding without friction: Mechanical energy conservation gives $mgh = \frac{1}{2}mV^2$, so $V^2 = 2gh$.

For a ring rolling without slipping: The moment of inertia is $I = mR^2$, and the velocity relation is $\omega = V_\text{ring}/R$. Energy conservation yields $mgh = \frac{1}{2}mV_\text{ring}^2 + \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2 = \frac{1}{2}mV_\text{ring}^2 + \frac{1}{2}mR^2(V_\text{ring}/R)^2 = mV_\text{ring}^2$. Thus, $V_\text{ring}^2 = gh$.

Substituting $gh = V^2/2$ from the sliding case, $V_\text{ring}^2 = V^2/2$, so $V_\text{ring} = V/\sqrt{2}$.

The linear velocity of the ring is $\boxed{\text{A}}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If $\vec{F}=(5 \hat{i}-10 \hat{j})$ and $\vec{r}=(4 \hat{i}-3 \hat{j})$, then the torque acting on the object will be
questions.solution:
Torque is given by the cross product $\vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F}$.

With $\vec{r} = 4\hat{i} - 3\hat{j}$ and $\vec{F} = 5\hat{i} - 10\hat{j}$, compute the determinant:

$\vec{\tau} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 4 & -3 & 0 \\ 5 & -10 & 0 \end{vmatrix} = \hat{k}((4)(-10) - (-3)(5)) = \hat{k}(-40 + 15) = -25\hat{k}$.

The result matches option D $(-25\hat{k})$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Four particles each of mass M are placed at the corners of a square of side L . The radius of gyration of the system about an axis perpendicular to the square and passing through its centre is
questions.solution:
The system consists of four particles of mass $M$ arranged at the corners of a square of side $L$. The rotation axis is perpendicular to the square's plane and passes through its center.

The distance $r$ from each corner to the center is half the diagonal length. The diagonal is $L\sqrt{2}$, so $r = L/\sqrt{2}$.

The moment of inertia for one particle about this axis is $Mr^2 = M(L^2 / 2) = ML^2 / 2$. For four identical particles, the total moment of inertia is $I_{\text{total}} = 4(ML^2 / 2) = 2ML^2$.

The total mass is $M_{\text{total}} = 4M$. The radius of gyration $k$ satisfies $I_{\text{total}} = M_{\text{total}} k^2$, so $2ML^2 = 4M k^2$.

Solving gives $k^2 = L^2 / 2$, hence $k = L / \sqrt{2}$.

The radius of gyration is $L / \sqrt{2}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A thin uniform rod of mass ' m ' and length ' L ' is pivoted at one end so that it can rotate in a vertical plane. The free end is held vertically above pivot and then released. The angular acceleration of the rod when it makes an angle ' $\theta$ ' with the vertical is [consider negligible friction at the pivot] ( $\mathrm{g}=$ acceleration due to gravity)
questions.solution:
For a uniform rod of length $L$ and mass $m$ pivoted at one end, the net torque about the pivot is due solely to gravity. The gravitational force $mg$ acts at the center of mass, located at a distance $L/2$ from the pivot. When the rod makes an angle $\theta$ with the vertical, the lever arm is $(L/2)\sin\theta$, yielding a torque $\tau = mg(L/2)\sin\theta$.

The moment of inertia about the pivot is $I = (1/3)mL^2$. Applying Newton's second law for rotation, $\tau = I\alpha$, gives:

$mg(L/2)\sin\theta = (1/3)mL^2 \alpha$

Solving for $\alpha$:

$\alpha = \frac{mg(L/2)\sin\theta}{(1/3)mL^2} = \frac{3g\sin\theta}{2L}$

This corresponds to option A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When a ceiling fan is switched off, its angular velocity falls to $\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{\mathrm{rd}}$ while it makes 24 rotations. How many more rotations will it make before coming to rest?
questions.solution:
Define angular velocity and deceleration: Let $\omega_0$ be the initial angular velocity and $\alpha$ the constant angular deceleration.

Phase 1: Velocity reduction to $\frac{\omega_0}{3}$ over 24 rotations. Using the kinematic relation $\omega^2 = \omega_0^2 + 2\alpha\theta$, where $\omega = \frac{\omega_0}{3}$ and $\theta = 24$ rotations:

$\left(\frac{\omega_0}{3}\right)^2 = \omega_0^2 + 2\alpha(24)$

$\frac{\omega_0^2}{9} - \omega_0^2 = 48\alpha$

$-\frac{8}{9}\omega_0^2 = 48\alpha$

$\alpha = -\frac{\omega_0^2}{54}$ rotations$^{-1}$

Phase 2: Rest from $\frac{\omega_0}{3}$. With $\omega' = \frac{\omega_0}{3}$, $\omega'' = 0$, and $\alpha$ as above, solve for additional rotations $\theta_2$:

$0 = \left(\frac{\omega_0}{3}\right)^2 + 2\left(-\frac{\omega_0^2}{54}\right)\theta_2$

$\frac{\omega_0^2}{9} = \frac{\omega_0^2}{27}\theta_2$

$\theta_2 = 3$ rotations

The fan makes 3 additional rotations before coming to rest.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Three point masses, each of mass ' $m$ ' are placed at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side ' $L$ '. The moment of inertia of the system about an axis passing through one of the vertices and parallel to the side joining other two vertices will be
questions.solution:
Consider the mass at vertex $A$ as shown in figure. Hence, M.I. about the line through A is, $\mathrm{I}=2 \mathrm{mh}^2$
From figure, $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{h}=\mathrm{L} \sin 60^{\circ}=\mathrm{L} \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ \therefore \quad & \mathrm{I}=2 \mathrm{~m} \times \frac{3}{4} \mathrm{~L}^2=\frac{3}{2} \mathrm{~mL}^2 \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two spheres of equal masses, one of which is a thin spherical shell and the other solid sphere, have the same moment of inertia about their respective diameters. The ratio of their radii is
questions.solution:
Let the radii of the thin spherical shell and the solid sphere be $R_1$ and $R_2$, respectively. Then, the moment of inertia of the shell about its diameter is given by,
$\mathrm{I}_{\text {shell }}=\frac{2}{3} \mathrm{MR}_1^2$...(i)
And the moment of inertia of the solid sphere is given by,
$\mathrm{I}_{\text {sphere }}=\frac{2}{5} \mathrm{MR}_2^2$...(ii)
Given that, the masses and moment of inertia for both the bodies are equal, then from equations (i) and (ii),
$\begin{array}{ll} 
& \frac{2}{3} M R_1^2=\frac{2}{5} \mathrm{MR}_2^2 \\
\therefore \quad & \frac{\mathrm{R}_1^2}{\mathrm{R}_2^2}=\frac{3}{5} \\
\therefore \quad & \mathrm{R}_1: \mathrm{R}_2=\sqrt{3}: \sqrt{5}
\end{array}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two loops $P$ and $Q$ of radii $R_1$ and $R_2$ are made from uniform metal wire of same material. $\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{P}}$ and $\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{Q}}$ be the moment of inertia of loop P and Q respectively then ratio $R_1 / R_2$ is $\left(\right.$ Given $\left.I_P / I_Q=27\right)$
questions.solution:
Two loops made from same material
$\mathrm{I}=\mathrm{MR}^2...(i)\mathrm{M}=\sigma .2 \pi \mathrm{R}$ Substituting in (i),
...( $\sigma$ is mass per unit length)
$\begin{aligned}
& I=\sigma \cdot 2 \pi \mathrm{R}^3 \\
\therefore \quad & \frac{\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{P}}}{\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{Q}}}= \\
& \frac{\sigma \cdot 2 \pi \mathrm{R}_1^3}{\sigma \cdot 2 \pi \mathrm{R}_2^3} \\
& \frac{\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{P}}}{\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{Q}}}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{R}_1}{\mathrm{R}_2}\right)^3 \\
& \frac{27}{1}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{R}_1}{\mathrm{R}_2}\right)^3 \quad \ldots(\text { (ii) } \\
\therefore \quad & \frac{\mathrm{R}_1}{\mathrm{R}_2}=\frac{3}{1}
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The power $(\mathrm{P})$ is supplied to a rotating body having moment of inertia ' I ' and angular acceleration ' $\alpha$ '. Its instantaneous angular velocity ' $\omega$ ' is
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \text { Power }=\frac{\text { Work done }}{\text { time }} \\ & P=\frac{\text { Torque } \times \text { angular displacement }}{\text { time }}=\tau \times \omega \\ & \ldots\left[\because \omega=\frac{\theta}{\mathrm{t}}\right] \\ & \therefore \quad P=I \alpha \omega \\ & \therefore \quad \omega=\frac{\mathrm{P}}{\mathrm{I} \alpha} \\ &=\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{I} \alpha)^{-1} \ldots(\because \tau=\mathrm{I} \alpha)\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body of mass $m$ slides down an incline and reaches the bottom with a velocity $V$. If the same mass were in the form of a disc which rolls down this incline, the velocity of the disc at bottom would have been
questions.solution:
Case 1: $\frac{1}{2} m V^2=m g h$ Case 2: $\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m}\left(\mathrm{v}^{\prime}\right)^2+\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{I} \omega^2=\mathrm{mgh}$ For disc, $\mathrm{I}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mR}^2\begin{aligned} \therefore \quad & \frac{1}{2} m\left(v^{\prime}\right)^2+\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{2} m R^2\right) \frac{\left(v^{\prime}\right)^2}{R^2}=m g h \\ & \frac{1}{2} m\left(v^{\prime}\right)^2+\frac{1}{4} m\left(v^{\prime}\right)^2=m g h \\ & \frac{3}{4} m\left(v^{\prime}\right)^2=m g h \quad \text {....(ii) } \end{aligned}$
From (i) and (ii), $\begin{aligned} & \frac{1}{2} m V^2=\frac{3}{4} m v^{\prime 2} \\ \therefore \quad & v^{\prime}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} V \end{aligned}$

By conservation of energy, $\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{I} \omega^2=\mathrm{Mgh}\therefore \quad \mathrm{h}=\frac{\mathrm{I} \omega^2}{2 \mathrm{Mg}}=\mathrm{h}...(i)$
The M.I of a uniform rod about an axis passing through its centre is $\frac{\mathrm{ML}^2}{12}$. As the axis passing through the end, using parallel axis theorem, $\mathrm{I}=\frac{\mathrm{ML}^2}{12}+\mathrm{M}\left(\frac{\mathrm{~L}}{2}\right)^2=\frac{\mathrm{ML}^2}{3}...(ii)$
Putting (ii) into (i), $h=\frac{L^2 \omega^2}{6 g}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
In case of rotational dynamics, which one of the following statements is correct?
$[\vec{\omega}=$ angular velocity, $\vec{v}=$ linear velocity
$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}=$ radius vector, $\vec{\alpha}=$ angular acceleration
$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}=$ linear acceleration, $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{L}}=$ angular momentum
$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}}=$ linear momentum, $\vec{\tau}=$ torque,
$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{f}}=$ centripetal force $]$
questions.solution:
Linear velocity \(\overrightarrow{(\mathrm{v})}\) :
The linear velocity of a point in rotational motion is given by the cross product of the angular velocity vector \((\vec{\omega})\) and the radius vector \(\overrightarrow{(r)}\) :
\(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}=\vec{\omega} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}\)
This shows the perpendicular relationship between linear velocity and both the radius vector and the angular velocity.
Angular acceleration (\(\vec{\alpha}\)):
The angular acceleration and its relation to linear acceleration can often be represented with:
\(\vec{\alpha}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}\)
Though, if specified to mean tangential component in a circular path, it directly relates to the tangential acceleration.
Angular momentum \((\overrightarrow{\mathrm{L}})\) :
The angular momentum of a particle with respect to a point is defined as:
\(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{L}}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}}\)
where \(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}}\) is the linear momentum (\(m v\)) of the particle.
Torque \((\vec{\tau})\) :
Torque is defined as the cross product of the radius vector \(\overrightarrow{(r)}\) and the force vector \(\overrightarrow{(\mathbf{f})}\) :
\(\vec{\tau}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{f}}\)
This defines the rotational effect of a force applied at a distance from a pivot.
Each component is consistent with the right-hand rule and the classical definitions in rotational dynamics.

$\therefore \quad \lambda=\frac{\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{P}}}{\mathrm{~L}_{\mathrm{p}}}=\frac{\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{Q}}}{\mathrm{~L}_{\mathrm{Q}}}\begin{array}{ll}\therefore \quad & \mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{P}}=\lambda \times \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{P}}=\lambda \times\left(2 \pi \mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{P}}\right)=2 \pi \mathrm{r} \lambda \\ & \text { Similarly, } \\ & \mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{Q}}=\lambda \times \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{Q}}=\lambda \times\left(2 \pi \mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{Q}}\right)=2 \pi(\mathrm{nr}) \lambda \\ & \text { Also, M.I. of circular loop } \mathrm{P} \text { is, } \\ & \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{P}}=\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{P}} \mathrm{r}^2=2 \pi \mathrm{r} \lambda(\mathrm{r})^2=2 \pi \mathrm{r}^3 \lambda \\ & \text { and that of loop } \mathrm{Q}, \\ & \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{Q}}=\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{Q}}(\mathrm{nr})^2=2 \pi(\mathrm{nr}) \lambda \times(\mathrm{nr})^2=2 \pi \mathrm{n}^3 \mathrm{r}^3 \lambda \\ & \mathrm{Given}^2 \text { that, } \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{Q}}=4 \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{P}} \\ \therefore \quad & 2 \pi \mathrm{n}^3 \mathrm{r}^3 \lambda=4 \times 2 \pi \mathrm{r}^3 \lambda \\ \therefore \quad \mathrm{n}^3=4 \\ \therefore \quad & \mathrm{n}=(4)^{\frac{1}{3}}=(2)^{\frac{2}{3}}\end{array}$

and,

We know moment of inertia for the ring $I_{\text {disc }}=\frac{1}{2} m R^2$ and the disc $I_{\text {ring }}=m R^2$ about its central axis perpendicular to its plane.
Using parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia about a tangential axis perpendicular to the plane can be easily obtained using,

The radius of gyration is defined as:

& \therefore K_{\text {disc }}=\sqrt{\frac{\frac{1}{2} m R^2+m R^2}{m}}=\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}} R \\
& \therefore K_{\text {ring }}=\sqrt{\frac{m R^2+m R^2}{m}}=\sqrt{2} R
\end{aligned}$
Thus, the ratio of the radius of gyration of a ring to that of a disc of same radius and mass, about a tangential axis perpendicular to the plane is:
$\frac{K_{\text {disc }}}{K_{\text {ring }}}=\frac{\sqrt{3 / 2}}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$

questions.solution:

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Five solid spheres each of mass $m$ and radius $r$ are rotating about an axis $A$ as shown in figure. Hence the moment of inertia of the system about the axis of rotation A-A' as shown in figure. Hence the moment of inertia of the system about the axis of rotation A-A' is
questions.solution:
Moment of inertia of a sphere about diameter is $\frac{2}{5} m r^2$
Moment of inertia of a sphere about it tangent using parallel axis theorem
$\begin{aligned} & I=I_{\mathrm{am}}+m r^2=\frac{2}{5} m r^2+m r^2=\frac{7}{5} m r^2 \\ & I_{\text {total }}=3\left(\frac{2}{5} m r^2\right)+2\left(\frac{7}{5} m r^2\right)=\frac{20}{5} m r^2=4 m r^2\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two circular loops $\mathrm{P}$ and $\mathrm{Q}$ of radii $r$ and $n r$ respectively are made from a uniform wire. Moment of inertia of $Q$ about its axis is four times that of $\mathrm{P}$ about its axis. The value of $n$ is
questions.solution:

Let $m$ be the mass per unit length of wire.
$\therefore m \times 2 \pi n r(n r)^2=4\left[(m 2 \pi r) r^2\right]$
Implies $n^3=4\Rightarrow n=4^{1 / 3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Consider a body shown in the figure, consisting of two identical balls, each of mass $\mathrm{M}$ connected by a light right rod. If an impulse $J=M V$ ( $V=$ linear velocity of ball)is imparted to the body at one of its ends, what would be its angular velocity?
questions.solution:
Impulse $J=\Delta P\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow M V=2 M v^{\prime}-0 \\ & \Rightarrow v^{\prime}=\frac{V}{2}\end{aligned}$
The rod will rotate about its COM.
Thus, $v^{\prime}=\omega R=\omega\left(\frac{L}{2}\right)\Rightarrow \omega=\frac{2 v^{\prime}}{L}=\frac{V}{L}$

questions.solution:
